identification.title: Psalm 46 (Lord of Hosts)
identification.notes: Written by Shane Barnard, Jennie Lee Riddle, Josh Miller and Josiah Warneking. CCLI 7053138. Part of the Worship Initiative's project of setting the psalter, and it stays close to the text it is named for.

claims.structuralNotes: Verses following the psalm's argument over a repeated chorus, with a bridge. The verses take Psalm 46's images in order — refuge, the shaking earth, the river, the nations in uproar — and the chorus is the psalm's own refrain.

claims.claim: God is a refuge and strength, a help in trouble.
claims.subject: God as refuge

claims.claim: The Lord of hosts is with his people.
claims.subject: God's presence

claims.claim: Though the earth gives way and mountains fall into the sea, the singer will not fear.
claims.subject: Fearlessness

claims.claim: God is exalted among the nations and over the earth.
claims.subject: God's sovereignty

claims.claim: The God of Jacob is a fortress for his people.
claims.subject: God as fortress

strengths.title: A psalm set rather than a psalm referenced
strengths.explanation: The song follows Psalm 46's argument in order and takes its chorus from the psalm's own refrain. A congregation singing it has the text in their mouths rather than a sentiment loosely inspired by it.
strengths.scriptureRationale: God is our refuge and strength, therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way.

strengths.title: Fearlessness argued from presence, not from circumstance
strengths.explanation: The reason given for not fearing is that God is with his people, not that the trouble will pass. The psalm's logic is preserved intact, and it is the harder and better comfort.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress — the refrain, kept as the refrain.

strengths.title: God exalted over nations, not just over the singer's trouble
strengths.explanation: The bridge widens from personal refuge to God's rule over the nations. It keeps the song from shrinking a public psalm into a private comfort.
strengths.scriptureRationale: I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.

strengths.title: Names catastrophe without softening it
strengths.explanation: Mountains falling into the sea is not domesticated into a difficult week. The song lets the psalm's worst case stand, which is what makes its confidence worth anything.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, its waters roar and foam.

doctrinesAffirmed: Fearlessness grounded in God rather than circumstance
theological.assessment: A psalm set faithfully rather than a song loosely inspired by one. It keeps the psalm's argument in order, its refrain as the refrain, and its worst case undomesticated — mountains falling into the sea, not a difficult week. The confidence it offers rests on God's presence rather than on the trouble passing. Nothing here needs correcting. As with the psalm, Christ is not named; a church using it will want the New Testament somewhere else in the service.

strengths.title: Says 'us', because the psalm does
strengths.explanation: The refrain is about what God is to a people, not to an individual. A congregation gets to make a corporate confession, which is rarer in current writing than it should be.

strengths.title: For a church in genuine trouble
strengths.explanation: Because the song names catastrophe rather than inconvenience, it can be sung by a congregation facing something serious without ringing false.

concerns.title: The chorus climbs and holds
concerns.explanation: The refrain sits high and sustains, which is where the song puts its weight. Rooms manage the verses comfortably and thin out at the line the song most wants them to sing.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly published in A and B flat. The chorus is the demanding part and it recurs; pitch the song for the refrain rather than the verses.

range.key: Commonly published in A and B flat
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The refrain repeats as the psalm's refrain repeats. What returns is a scriptural sentence rather than a hook, which is repetition doing its proper work.
communal.assessment: Corporate by construction and usable in real trouble, which is a good combination. The practical caution is the chorus: it sits high and it is the line the congregation most needs to sing, so the key deserves care.

strengths.title: Follows the psalm's own order
strengths.explanation: Trouble, then presence, then God's exaltation. Because the sequence is the text's, the song's argument is coherent in a way loosely-assembled songs are not.

strengths.title: The object is named and specific
strengths.explanation: The Lord of hosts, the God of Jacob: this is not an unspecified 'You'. A hearer knows precisely who is being sung about.

concerns.title: 'Lord of hosts' passes unexplained
concerns.explanation: The title carries armies and heavenly ranks behind it, and a modern hearer may take it as a general honorific. The song does not unpack it, though the psalm does not either.

clarity.assessment: Clear and specifically addressed. The psalm's sequence keeps the argument coherent and the divine titles rule out any doubt about the object. Only 'Lord of hosts' goes by without its meaning being opened up.

synthesis.summary: A psalm set faithfully rather than loosely referenced: the argument stays in order, the refrain stays the refrain, and the worst case is left undomesticated — mountains falling into the sea, not a difficult week. Its confidence rests on God's presence rather than the trouble passing. As with the psalm, Christ is not named.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The refuge and the catastrophe the verses set almost unaltered.
The refrain the song keeps as its chorus.
Exaltation among the nations, which the bridge widens to.
